title: UNC basketball player sues NCAA seeking additional year of eligibility

 UNC basketball player sues NCAA seeking additional year of eligibility
 Cameron Fens, who transferred to UNC from South Dakota, is asking an Orange County judge to allow him to play for the Tar Heels this season. Fens has already played four seasons of college basketball.

 By Brian Murphy, WRAL News
 An Orange County Superior Court judge will decide today whether a North Carolina men's basketball player will be able to play for the team while the NCAA determines his eligibility status. 
 North Carolina men’s basketball player Cameron Fens — who has played four NCAA seasons, though none for the Tar Heels — filed a lawsuit Wednesday, asking an Orange County Superior Court judge to declare him eligible to play another season.
 Other WRAL Top Stories
 Fens, a 7-foot center, is seeking a temporary restraining order prohibiting the NCAA and others from treating him as ineligible or from punishing North Carolina if it plays Fens. Fens is also seeking a preliminary injunction that would allow him to play through the court’s final decision. Judge Alyson Grine told attorneys she would have a decision on the temporary restraining order later this afternoon. 
 “He is physical and strong, and he is a skilled player,” UNC coach Michael Malone said in an affidavit filed with the court. “If he were eligible, he would be a regular part of our rotation.”
 The NCAA, the only defendant in the case, didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. A hearing is set for Thursday at 11 a.m.
 Fens played two seasons at Illinois-Chicago and two seasons at South Dakota before transferring to UNC for a fifth season. Fens averaged 14.4 points and 8.7 rebounds per game for South Dakota last season.
 The lawsuit says that Fens’ 2024-25 season shouldn’t count against him as a year of eligibility because of a misdiagnosis of a broken foot. Fens says he broke his foot in the seventh game of that season, but it was misdiagnosed as a “soft-tissue injury.” He played with the injury until Jan. 16, 2025, according to the lawsuit. Because he played in more than 30% of the season’s games, the NCAA’s guidelines allow for relief only for extraordinary circumstances, such as “medical misdiagnosis,” according to the lawsuit.
 South Dakota applied for a hardship waiver in February. It was still pending when he transferred to UNC. The NCAA denied a waiver on Oct. 20.
 The NCAA has implemented five years of eligibility for players moving forward, but Fens and other players that entered college in 2022 aren’t subject to the new rule. Many players from that class who played four seasons have sued the NCAA — and many have been granted an additional year of eligibility, including North Carolina football kicker Rece Verhoff , three members of UNC’s women’s field hockey team and former UNC basketball star Seth Trimble, who is playing for Louisville.
 Fens argues that the NCAA can’t show that granting one more fifth-year player eligibility would disrupt competition.
 In his affidavit, Malone mentioned several fifth-year players on teams that UNC will compete against this season, including Trimble, NC State’s Ven-Allen Lubin, West Virginia’s Brenen Lorient and Javan Buchanan, Syracuse’s Amarri Monroe, Wake Forest’s Justin Abson and Miami’s Malik Reneau.
 “I understand that each of these players is competing under a court order,” Malone said. “Playing Cameron would put him on the same footing as the fifth-year players we will compete against.”
 UNC's next game is Friday vs. Marshall. The Tar Heels are 3-1 on the season.
